notes: House of Lords judgment on parental means and section 2 CSDPA; statutory framework and outcome are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Spink v Wandsworth: parental means and disabled children's home adaptations

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970
Housing, Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Health and Social Services and Social Security Adjudications Act 1983

key_facts: Two profoundly disabled boys needed home aids and adaptations including lifts, an adapted bathroom and a safe play area.
Wandsworth accepted section 2 of the 1970 Act applied but said it need not fund adaptations if the parents had sufficient resources, assessed by reference to disabled facilities grant means-testing.
The parents' earlier DFG application had found a contribution of over £40,000 and they disputed intrusive financial investigation.
Permission had been granted only on the aids and adaptations issue, not on the separate care package dispute.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review after permission was granted on whether a local authority may consider parental financial resources under section 2 of the 1970 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the local authority was entitled to have regard to the parents' financial resources when deciding whether it was necessary for it to make arrangements for aids and adaptations.
enrichment.ratio: Section 2 of the 1970 Act involves three stages—identifying needs, deciding whether it is necessary for the authority itself to meet them, and then the duty to make arrangements—and at the second stage an authority may lawfully consider whether needs could reasonably be met by parents or another third party, including where a DFG might be available, provided Convention rights are respected in the particular case.
legal_issues: Whether parental financial resources may be taken into account under section 2 when deciding necessity
Relationship between disabled facilities grants and section 2 welfare duties
Whether section 17 charging powers are inconsistent with a needs-based duty
Whether Article 8 required a different construction of section 2
index_terms: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act
linked_authorities: R v Gloucestershire County Council, ex parte Barry [1997] AC 584
R (A and B) v East Sussex CC [2003] EWHC 167 (Admin)
R (Fay) v Essex County Council [2004] EWHC 879 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Final House of Lords disposition on the statutory construction issue is explicit and detailed.

notes: Landmark preliminary ruling on expert witness costs liability; reasoning is extensive and explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Symes litigation: preliminary ruling on expert costs liability
key_facts: Administrators in the Symes partnership litigation sought costs against Dr Zamar, a psychiatrist who had opined that Mr Symes lacked capacity since 1980.
Peter Smith J had rejected Dr Zamar's capacity evidence at trial and joined him for costs only under CPR 48.2.
The Administrators alleged Dr Zamar acted recklessly and in serious breach of CPR 35 expert duties, including failing to reconsider his opinion when further material was provided.
Mr Symes was bankrupt, making recovery from the litigant impracticable and prompting the application against the expert.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary hearing on whether an enquiry should proceed into whether a non-party expert witness may be ordered to pay costs for gross dereliction of duties to the court.
enrichment.outcome: The judge declined to set aside the joinder order or dismiss the application; Dr Zamar had a case to answer at a further enquiry, though no finding of breach or costs liability was made.
enrichment.ratio: An expert witness's general immunity from suit for evidence given does not preclude, in an exceptional case of flagrant reckless breach of CPR 35 duties, a non-party costs order under the court's section 51 discretion; the CPR declaration and contempt sanctions already warn experts that breach may have serious consequences.
legal_issues: Whether an expert witness may be subject to a non-party costs order
Interaction between witness immunity and section 51 costs discretion
Whether Symphony Group supports costs orders against witnesses
Whether the trial judge should recuse himself after criticising the expert's evidence
linked_authorities: Symphony Group Plc v Hodgson [1994] QB 179
Stanton v Callaghan [2000] 1 QB 75
National Justice Compania Naviera SA v Prudential Assurance Co Ltd (The Ikarian Reefer) [1993] 2 Lloyd's Rep 68

confidence.notes: Preliminary threshold ruling only; merits of any costs order were expressly reserved.

notes: Case stated on exclusion of prosecution submissions; procedural history and appellate answers are clear.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Ayres: magistrates wrongly excluded prosecution on abuse application
key_facts: Michael Ayres faced summary charges of assaulting police, disorderly conduct and being drunk and disorderly after an incident in Ealing.
The CPS repeatedly failed to comply with magistrates' disclosure directions, including primary disclosure, disciplinary records, CCTV originals and a medical report.
On 4 May 2004 the justices heard only the defence on an abuse of process application after excluding the prosecution for failing to file a skeleton argument.
The justices initially refused a stay, then revised their decision and stayed the proceedings for prosecutorial impropriety.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated by the Director of Public Prosecutions against a magistrates' decision to stay proceedings and to exclude the prosecution from oral submissions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the stated questions; the justices were wrong to exclude the prosecution and could not properly decide abuse of process without hearing it, though the court expressed grave concern about CPS defaults and did not remit the case.
enrichment.ratio: Criminal proceedings are essentially oral and it is unjust, save in exceptional circumstances, to shut out a party from making submissions on abuse of process merely for failure to lodge a skeleton, especially where serious charges are involved and the prosecution is present and ready to be heard.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates could exclude the prosecution from an abuse of process hearing
Whether it was unfair to try the defendant given sustained CPS non-compliance with directions
Whether proceedings should be stayed for abuse of process
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department, ex parte Al-Mehdawi [1990] 1 AC 876

confidence.notes: Answers to the stated questions are direct; broader merits of any future abuse application were not finally resolved.

notes: Short unrepresented prison status challenge; follows Potter and outcome is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Hamblett: refusal of enhanced status for denying sex offender treatment
key_facts: Mr Hamblett was serving a 15-year sentence for numerous sexual offences and sought enhanced prison privileges.
Enhanced status was refused because he would not engage with a Sexual Offenders Treatment Programme assessment and declined an Enhanced Thinking Skills course.
He persistently denied his offences despite exhausted appeals and a closed CCRC file, though he had previously claimed to be an appellant.
The Prison Ombudsman's recommendations had been implemented and did not assist his claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review, without representation, of refusal to accord enhanced status at HM Prison Frankland.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review refused; refusal of enhanced status for non-engagement with SOTP where the prisoner denied guilt was reasonable and lawful.
enrichment.ratio: Following R(Potter), a prison governor may lawfully withhold enhanced status from a convicted sex offender who persistently denies his offences and is therefore unsuitable for an SOTP, because enhanced status rewards addressing offending behaviour.
legal_issues: Whether refusal of SOTP assessment for a persistent denier was unlawful
Whether requiring an Enhanced Thinking Skills course was unreasonable
Whether the Prison Service failed to comply with Ombudsman recommendations
linked_authorities: R(Potter and ors) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] EWHC Admin 1041

confidence.notes: Short judgment applying established authority with no disputed fact findings.

notes: Leading Court of Appeal guidance on section 29 NHS Reform Act references; detailed and authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Ruscillo and Truscott: section 29 CRHP reference appeals

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service Reform and Health Care Professions Act 2002

key_facts: Dr Ruscillo was acquitted by the GMC Professional Conduct Committee of serious professional misconduct after limited admissions and minimal evidence on context.
The Council for the Regulation of Health Care Professionals referred the acquittal to the High Court as unduly lenient.
Nurse Steven Truscott admitted accessing pornography on a hospital computer on a paediatric adolescent unit and received an NMC caution rather than removal from the register.
The Council appealed Truscott's sanction as unduly lenient; Collins J dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two conjoined Court of Appeal appeals on the construction and operation of section 29 references against GMC and NMC disciplinary decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Ruscillo appeal dismissed: section 29 permits references against acquittals where criteria are met; Truscott appeal dismissed and the caution was held not unduly lenient on the evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Section 29 allows the Council to refer an acquittal or inadequate penalty where the decision is unduly lenient and public protection requires review; on appeal the High Court asks whether the penalty decision was wrong because no reasonable disciplinary tribunal could have imposed it, but may consider fresh evidence where under-prosecution prevented the tribunal from assessing risk.
legal_issues: Whether section 29 permits appeals against acquittals
Whether the High Court applies the section 29 undue leniency test or ordinary CPR 52.11 grounds
Whether under-prosecution and fresh evidence may found a reference
Whether Truscott's caution was unduly lenient
index_terms: Council for the Regulation of Health Care Professionals

Council for the Regulation of Health Care Professionals v General Medical Council and Dr Solanke [2004] EWHC 944 (Admin)
Lomas v Parle [2004] 1 All ER 1173

notes: Detailed costs judgment after capacity issue; exceptional Part 20 analysis is clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Symes capacity issue: costs between Administrators and solicitors
key_facts: Peter Smith J held Mr Symes had capacity throughout the relevant periods after a five-day issue trial.
Solicitor firms were joined to the capacity issue so their liability under Yonge v Toynbee could be determined in one hearing if capacity were lacking.
The Administrators succeeded on capacity but Mr Symes was bankrupt, making costs recovery difficult.
The Solicitor Respondents sought costs from the Administrators as successful Part 20 defendants; the Administrators argued Symes should pay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs hearing following determination of preliminary issues as to Mr Symes' mental capacity in longstanding Chancery proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Mr Symes ordered to pay the Administrators' costs of the Issue; in exceptional circumstances the Solicitor Respondents' costs were also ordered against Mr Symes rather than the Administrators.
enrichment.ratio: Although joinder of former solicitors to a capacity issue may resemble a Part 20 claim, where the incapacity allegation was raised by the defendant, stymied the action and necessarily drew solicitors into an in rem-style enquiry, the normal rule that a Part 20 claimant pays a successful Part 20 defendant may be displaced and the impecunious party who caused the issue may bear all costs.
legal_issues: Who should pay the costs of the capacity issue as between Administrators and Solicitor Respondents
Whether joinder was properly treated as a Part 20 claim
Whether Johnson v Ribbins/Arkin principles applied
Liability of Mr Symes for all parties' costs
linked_authorities: Johnson v Ribbins [1977] 1 WLR 158
Arkin v Borchard Lines Ltd (No 3) [2004] 1 Lloyd's Rep 636
Yonge v Toynbee [1910] 1 KB 215

confidence.notes: Final costs orders are explicit though the exceptional departure from Part 20 norms is fact-specific.

notes: Interlocutory libel rulings on special damages and mode of trial; reserved judgment is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Collins Stewart v FT: strike-out of market-cap libel damages
key_facts: Collins Stewart sued the Financial Times over a 27 August 2003 article reporting a former analyst's FSA complaint about conflicts of interest and analyst pressure.
The claimants pleaded a 16% fall in Plc's share price and about £141 million loss of market capitalisation as part of their damages case.
The FT applied to strike out paragraphs 3-6 of the Particulars of Special Damage relying on share price movement and reflective loss principles.
Eady J had ordered a split trial with liability and general damages before a jury and special damages later; the FT sought all damages before a judge alone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory applications to strike out parts of the particulars of special damage and to vary the mode of trial of damages in a jury libel action.
enrichment.outcome: Paragraphs 3-6 of the particulars of special damage were struck out; Eady J's order was varied so liability would be tried by judge and jury first and all damages issues, if they arose, by judge alone.
enrichment.ratio: In a corporate libel claim a pleading based on market capitalisation/share price movement is not a free-standing measure of special damage and may infringe the reflective loss principle; where there is no personal claimant and general and special business damages are closely linked, damages are better assessed together by a judge after liability is determined.
legal_issues: Whether share price or market capitalisation loss is recoverable special damage in libel
Application of the reflective loss principle to corporate claimants
Whether general and special damages should be split between jury and judge
Proper test on a strike-out application under CPR 3.4
linked_authorities: Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Interlocutory rulings only; liability and remaining damages were still to be tried.

notes: Article 8 prison telephone policy challenge; proportionality analysis and refusal are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Taylor v Risley: blanket PIN telephone enabling at prison
key_facts: Mr Taylor, a life prisoner for murder, challenged Risley's blanket call-enabling telephone system requiring pre-approved PIN numbers.
Risley had high drug misuse rates and an integrated regime mixing public protection prisoners with others.
The governor said enabling the whole prison was necessary to restrict drug dealing and prevent PIN sharing abuse if mixed enabling/barring regimes operated.
Taylor argued the policy fell outside draft PSO 4400 mandatory enabling categories and interfered disproportionately with Article 8 family contact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the governor's decision to operate a prison-wide call enabling regime at HM Prison Risley.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the blanket call enabling regime was a proportionate interference with Article 8 rights in the circumstances of this prison at this time.
enrichment.ratio: Applying Daly, a blanket prison telephone policy may be justified where the governor adduces concrete operational reasons—here serious drug misuse and the impossibility of a mixed enabling/barring system without PIN abuse—and the restrictions remain within Rule 34 and a context-specific proportionality assessment.
legal_issues: Whether blanket call enabling was outside applicable Prison Service guidance
Whether the policy was a disproportionate interference with Article 8
Whether a mixed enabling and barring regime was workable
Whether the 20p charge for changing enabled numbers was unreasonable
linked_authorities: R (Daly) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] UKHL 26
R (Hirst) v Secretary of State [2002] EWHC 602 (Admin)
de Freitas v Permanent Secretary of Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Lands and Housing [1999] 1 AC 69

confidence.notes: Fact-specific proportionality decision explicitly limited to Risley at the relevant time.

notes: Statutory construction of section 96 SSFA 1998; permission refused on clear wording.

enrichment.short_title: B v Hertfordshire: section 96 direction when one school place offered
key_facts: B, a highly able eleven-year-old with written expression difficulties, failed the entrance exam for preferred selective school X.
Hertfordshire offered him a place at nearer non-selective school Y after the Independent Appeal Panel dismissed his appeal against school X.
His parents asked the local authority to direct admission to school X under section 96, which the authority refused saying it would not override the appeal panel.
The authority later argued section 96 was not engaged because B had not been refused admission to every suitable school within reasonable distance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review of refusal to exercise the section 96 direction power.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused and application dismissed; section 96 was not engaged because B had been offered a place at a suitable school within reasonable distance and 'each school' means every such school.
enrichment.ratio: Section 96(1) is engaged only where a child has been refused admission to, or permanently excluded from, every school within reasonable distance that provides suitable education; where one suitable school has offered a place the power does not arise even if another preferred school has refused admission.
legal_issues: Whether 'each school' in section 96(1) means 'every' or 'a' school
Whether section 96 was engaged when one suitable school place had been offered
Whether the authority unlawfully fettered its discretion by refusing to override the appeal panel

confidence.notes: Pure statutory construction with a clear negative permission decision.

notes: Case stated on breath test failures; clear corrective answers and partial remittal.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Swan: failure to provide breath specimens at roadside and station
key_facts: Mr Swan, a retired Sussex detective sergeant, was stopped on the A27 and asked to provide a roadside breath specimen under section 6.
The justices found he was never given a real opportunity because the device was neither proffered nor produced, though he was agitated and used delaying tactics.
At the police station he was abusive, preoccupied with wrist injuries from handcuffs and insisted on photographs before providing a section 7 specimen until the machine timed out.
The justices acquitted on both counts, treating his wrist-photograph request as not an outrageous condition under Mackey.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Prosecution appeal by case stated against acquittals on failing to provide breath specimens under sections 6 and 7 of the 1988 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; directed conviction on the section 6 roadside offence and remittal on the section 7 station offence for consideration of a reasonable excuse based on medical unfitness.
enrichment.ratio: A section 6 requirement is satisfied by words alone without physically producing the device; rude and delaying conduct may amount to failure without reasonable excuse, and at the station imposing preconditions such as guaranteed photographs before blowing is not a reasonable excuse and may be treated as failure even if not 'outrageous' under Mackey.
legal_issues: Whether physical production of the breath test device is required for a section 6 request
Whether delaying and abusive conduct amounted to failure without reasonable excuse
Whether Mackey requires an 'outrageous' condition before finding failure at the police station
Whether medical unfitness could provide reasonable excuse on remittal
linked_authorities: R v Ferguson [1970] 54 Cr App R 415
Mackey [1977] RTR 146

confidence.notes: Section 6 disposition is final by direction; section 7 remains subject to remittal on reasonable excuse.
